Any of a number of immunoassay-based techniques that can be completed outside a laboratory in less than 30 minutes.

A modified polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique in which DNA amplification is detected and quantified as the PCR reaction progresses, through the use of fluorescent DNA probes in the reaction mixture.
A method in which a probe is bounced off of the surface of the cornea, creating an induction current that is used to calculate intraocular pressure.
The spectroscopic analysis of light reflected from a polished sample.
A method to measure the refractive index (propensity for light to bend) of a sample. (NCI)
A genomic microarray-based method that analyzes two restriction enzyme digested full genomes to identify regions in the genome that have undergone large scale variation.
A type of functional magnetic resonance imaging that is performed on an organ in the absence of a stimulus or task. (NCI)
A technique that analyzes restriction fragments of target DNA sequences to detect polymorphisms.
An imaging technique in which X-ray images of the renal pelvis and urinary tract obtained after injection of a radiopaque substance into the ureter, usually done via a cystoscope.

A high-throughput antibody-based functional proteomic microarray that can quantify basal protein expression and characterize as well as quantify post-translational modifications in a series of samples of body fluids or those derived from tissue or cellular lysates. (NCI)
A molecular biology technique used to recreate and amplify complementary DNA (cDNA) from total RNA or messenger RNA (mRNA), using reverse transcriptase and DNA polymerase.

Radioimmunoassay (RIA) is an immunological technique, which quantitatively determines antigen and antibody concentrations, using a radioactively labeled substance (radioligand), either directly or indirectly.

A technique that assesses auditory function by comparing sound conduction through air versus the mastoid bone, in which a vibrating tuning fork (at 512Hz) is placed on the mastoid bone and the subject indicates when they can no longer hear the vibration, at which point the still vibrating tuning fork is moved 1-2cm from the auditory canal and the subject again indicates when they can no longer hear the fork.
A microscopy staining method that utilizes both cationic and anionic dyes (typically methylene blue and eosin Y, respectively) for the morphological assessment of cells in a biological specimen.

A standardized method of color vision testing that is a shortened version of the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test (FM100), using every third of the FM100's 85 color caps that are arranged in rows of four color families.
A measurement methodology in which a ruler device is used for measuring distance, consisting of an elongated piece of material marked with units of length.

A microscopy staining method that utilizes a modified trichrome stain to determine the presence of microspordial, sporulating species. This staining technique substitutes aniline blue for the fast green counterstain of the original trichrome staining method and decreased levels of phosphotungstic acid in the reagent.
A type of enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay that uses separate capture and detection antibodies such that the antigen is bound between the two antibodies.

A DNA sequencing technique in which a mixture of deoxynucleosidetriphosphates (dNTPs) and chain-terminating dNTPs (which are radioactively or fluorescently labeled) are combined within the reaction mixture. Once the polymerase chain reaction is complete the DNA strands are separated by size and the labeled chain terminating dNTPs can be read in sequence by the investigator or a machine.
An electron microscopy imaging technique that is utilized to examine structural components of a sample by passing electrons through a specimen that has been coated with a heavy metal.
A method to assess tear production in which filter paper is placed inside the lower eyelid for a period of time and moisture content is measured.

An imaging technique that uses a small dose of a radioactive chemical (isotope) called a tracer that can detect sites of cancer growth, trauma, infection or degenerative disorders. The tracer, which is either injected into a vein or swallowed, travels through the bloodstream to the target organ, and emits gamma rays, which are detected by a gamma camera and analyzed by a computer to form an image of the target organ. (NCI)

An analytical technique in which a mass spectrometer is used to measure the atomic weight of sputtered ionized atoms (secondary ions) that are ejected from a solid surface after application of a beam of high energy primary ions.
A technique in which one evaluates their own actions or performance.
An individual's perspective or subjective interpretation of an event or information.

A type of reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction combined with electrophoresis. After real-time PCR reaction, amplified gene products undergo electrophoretic separation and the level of expression of the target gene is determined by measuring the intensity of the gel bands corresponding to the target gene amplicon normalized to a housekeeping, internal control gene.
terms.preferredTerm: Semi-Quantitative Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction
terms.submissionValue: SEMI-QUANTITATIVE REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION

terms.definition: A modified polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique in which primer pair(s) are used to select a highly specific nucleotide sequence of interest, which will be the only sequence amplified.
terms.preferredTerm: Allele Specific Primer Polymerase Chain Reaction
terms.submissionValue: SEQUENCE SPECIFIC PRIMER POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION

terms.definition: A method that uses PCR amplification of specific nucleotides to produce templates and primers that are used to provide the entirety of the nucleotide sequence of a specific DNA strand, allowing for reliable and thorough genotyping of the allele in question.

A modified polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique that uses distinct probes, specifically synthesized according to the polymorphic region of the gene of interest, to detect nucleotide differences during genotype testing.
terms.preferredTerm: Sequence-specific Oligonucleotide Probe Polymerase Chain Reaction
terms.submissionValue: SEQUENCE-SPECIFIC OLIGONUCLEOTIDE PROBE POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION

terms.definition: A process to identify and determine the primary structure of, and the order of constituents in a biopolymer. Used when a more specific sequencing methodology is not specified.
A method in which a nano-electrospray produces charging agents that collide with analyte molecules in gas-phase, creating an ionized vapor that is then analyzed via high resolution mass spectrometry.
terms.preferredTerm: Secondary Electrospray Ionization High-resolution Mass Spectrometry
synonyms: Secondary Electrospray Ionization High-resolution Mass Spectrometry

terms.definition: A method of screening for sickle cell disease or trait in which sodium dithionite or a similar chemical is used to lyse red blood cells in a blood sample. This allows any hemoglobin S, which does not dissolve easily in plasma, to form crystals that visibly cloud the plasma.
A type of solid-phase multiplex assay that uses microbeads coated with a recombinant or purified antigen that will identify a single antibody.
A type of enzyme-linked immunoassay in which single molecules can be detected through the use of femtomolar-sized reaction chambers and an excess of fluorescently labeled antibody-bound beads.

An assay technique where a primer is hybridized adjacent to the interrogated variant site and is extended by deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) polymerase to incorporate a complementary base that can be labeled for detection.
A type of spiral computed tomography that employs only one detector and produces one image (slice). (NCI)
A modified polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique followed by electrophoresis such that DNA molecular weights and three-dimensional structures are used to identify mutations.
A type of in situ hybridization that uses a hybridization probe linked to an enzyme that elicits neutralization and deposition of silver onto the probe target site.
Gel permeation or sieve chromatography that is performed on porous gels that separate solutes on the basis of size.
A method of capturing images using a horizontally mounted microscope with an attached slit lamp.
A method for examining the anterior segment of the eye using a slit lamp.
A diagrammatic method to test visual acuity that uses the Sloan optotypes and a 1.25% contrast level.
A diagrammatic method to test visual acuity that uses the Sloan optotypes and a 100% contrast level.
A diagrammatic method to test visual acuity that uses the Sloan optotypes and a 2.5% contrast level.
The action of spreading a thin layer of material across a surface.
A technique to assess puffing behavior in smokers, using a smoking topography (ST) device.

A diagrammatic method to test visual acuity, which uses a chart containing 11 lines of Sloan optotypes in varying sizes with the largest located at the top of the chart and decreasing in size toward the bottom of the chart.
A genomic microarray-based method able to detect single nucleotide polymorphisms.

A hemoglobin estimation technique that utilizes sodium lauryl sulphate, a surfactant that lyses erythrocytes. The released hemoglobin converts to methemoglobin and forms a sodium lauryl sulphate-methemoglobin complex with a characteristic light absorbance spectrum, which is detected by photometry.
terms.submissionValue: SODIUM LAUREL SULFATE-METHEMOGLOBIN COMPLEX DETECTION PHOTOMETRY

terms.definition: A type of tomography in which gamma photon-emitting radionuclides are administered to the patient and then detected by one or more gamma cameras rotated around the patient. From the series of two-dimensional images produced, a three-dimensional image can be created by computer reconstruction.
A dual-modality imaging technique that merges data from single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and computed tomography (CT) to provide structural and functional information.
terms.preferredTerm: Single Photon Tomography and Computed Tomography Scan

terms.definition: A technique used to calculate the transmittance of light through a material.

A noninvasive photographic technique used to visualize and examine the corneal endothelium, in which a source of light is projected onto the cornea and the subsequent image reflected from the optical interface between the corneal endothelium and the aqueous humor is captured.
A type of spiral CT scan in which the images are not enhanced by the addition of contrast agents into the body.
A method of examining body organs by scanning them with X rays and using a computer to construct a series of cross-sectional scans along a single axis.
A method used to measure the breathing capacity of the lung by means of a spirometer.
An eye examination technique that utilizes test objects with gradually increasing luminance that are positioned at fixed locations across the visual field to determine the threshold of visibility.

An echocardiographic technique in which an image of the heart is produced by ultrasonography under conditions (e.g., exercise, pharmacologic agents or pacing) intended to elicit signs and symptoms of myocardial ischemia.
A quantum optical-electrical phenomena consisting of an alteration in light reflectance as a result of binding of molecules to a surface from which total internal reflection is occurring.
An MRI-based imaging technique that uses phase differences between tissues, due to differences in magnetic susceptibilities, to produce an enhanced contrast magnitude image.

A technique that measures an evoked potential caused by a visual stimulus and recorded by an electroencephalogram, and which is used for those individuals who are unable to provide a verbal response to questions, including infants, toddlers, and other non-verbal individuals.
A technique for measuring anatomical densities in which a single X-ray beam, whose low and high energy is separated, is aimed at the anatomical location of interest and x-ray absorption is assessed.
A DNA sequencing technique in which selected regions of an individual's genome are sequenced.
An RNA sequencing technique in which selected RNA transcripts of an individual's genome are sequenced.

A type of functional magnetic resonance imaging that images dynamic changes in brain tissue while the subject performs a task or experiences a sensory stimulus designed to target specific cognitive processes.

A diagrammatic method to test visual acuity that uses a set of cards with parallel lines, used for those individuals who are unable to provide a verbal response to questions, including infants, toddlers, and other non verbal individuals.

A modification of the Ivy method for assessing bleeding time in which the individual wears a blood pressure cuff inflated to 40mmHg, a controlled incision is made using an automatic blade on the volar surface of the arm (thus standardizing the incision size), and blood is drawn off of the incision site with blotting paper every 30 seconds until bleeding stops.
A piece of chemically treated medium designed to react in the presence of specific amounts of a trigger substance.
A mass spectrometry method in which chemically purified samples are heated to create positively ionized atoms that are then accelerated by an electric field and mass separated by an electromagnet.
A blood smear technique used to make a thick blood smear on a microscope slide which is generally used to look for blood parasites such as those causing malaria.
A blood smear technique used to make a thin blood smear on a microscope slide which is generally used to look for blood parasites such as those causing malaria.

A method of testing the efficiency of blood coagulation in which the amplitude of movement of a pin suspended in the center of an oscillating blood sample, or the vertical movement of the meniscus of a vibrating blood sample, is measured over time and analyzed to assess the dynamics and physical properties of blood clot formation in a low shear environment.

A group of methods in which an analyte amount is determined based on its stoichiometric reaction with a reagent of established concentration that is introduced to a sample gradually until the analyte is consumed. (ScienceDirect)
A microscopy staining method that utilizes toluidine blue, a solution composed of tolonium chloride, to determine the presence of mast cells, lignin, proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans.
A method in which pressure is applied to the surface of the cornea in order to flatten a prespecified area of the membrane.
A procedure involving irradiation of the whole body.
A diagnostic radiologic test that involves the examination of the entire body in a single procedure.

A method of assessing capillary fragility that is used in the diagnosis of hemorrhagic fevers. After taking a blood pressure measurement, the cuff is inflated to a point midway between the assessed systolic and diastolic pressures and maintained for five minutes; the cuff is then released and, after two minutes, the number of petechiae below the antecubital fossa are counted.
An in vitro assay to measure antibody in a biological specimen capable of protecting cells against the effect of a specific toxin.
An ultrasound imaging technique in which the ultrasound probe is pressed against the skin of the abdomen in order to create an image of the abdominal organs.
A technique used to selectively replicate nucleic acid sequences from RNA templates using reverse transcriptase and RNA polymerase.
A cardiac ultrasound performed by passing a specialized probe containing a transducer into the patient's esophagus.
An electron microscopy imaging technique that is utilized to examine structural components of a sample by passing electrons through the specimen.
A non-invasive cardiac ultrasound performed by placing the transducer on the chest.

A technique in which sound waves are sent out by an ultrasound probe that has been inserted in the vagina and a computer uses the ultrasound echoes to create an image of the female reproductive organs.

A microscopy staining method that utilizes two or more colored, acidic dyes of contrasting colors. Masson trichrome is a mixture of three dyes including aniline blue, Beibrich scarlet and Weigert's iron hematoxylin. Other related, modified trichrome staining methods include Lillie's trichrome, Gomori's trichrome and Mallory's trichrome.
A type of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in which images are taken during three distinct timing points (phases) following the injection of contrast material: arterial, venous, and delayed.
A type of computed tomography (CT) in which images are taken during three distinct timing points (phases) following the injection of contrast material: arterial, venous, and delayed.
A microscopy staining method that utilizes trypan blue, an acid azo dye that can traverse the cell membrane of dead cells and is used to differentiate between living and dead cells. (NCI)
A method to quantify the opaqueness of a liquid using a turbidimeter, by measuring the decrease in light intensity due to the scattering effect of suspended particles in the liquid sample.

A genomic microarray-based method using cDNA from two samples, labeled with two separate fluorophores/dyes at different emission wavelengths, and hybridized to a single microarray. The relative fluorescence intensity of each dye is being measured.
A technique that measures energy transmission through the middle ear using a tympanometer.
An analytical technique where ultra-high performance liquid chromatography is coupled to accelerated mass spectrometry in order to separate, identify, and quantify substances in a sample.
terms.preferredTerm: Ultra High Performance Liquid Chromatography/Accelerator Mass Spectrometry

terms.definition: An analytical technique where ultra-high performance liquid chromatography is coupled to tandem mass spectrometry in order to separate, identify, and quantify substances in a sample.
terms.preferredTerm: Ultra High-performance Liquid Chromatography/Tandem Mass Spectrometry

terms.definition: A noninvasive technique that is used to measure organ or tissue stiffness. An ultrasound wave is passed into the organ or tissue from a small transducer on the end of an ultrasound probe which measures the velocity of the shear wave (in meters per second) as this wave passes through the organ or tissue. The shear wave velocity can then be converted into organ or tissue stiffness. This technique may be used as an alternative to organ or tissue biopsy.
A technique in which high-frequency sound waves are bounced off internal organs and the echo pattern is converted into a 2 dimensional picture of the structures beneath the transducer.
A microscopy staining method that utilizes uranyl acetate, a water insoluble yellow crystalline solid, which is used as a negative stain in electron microscopy.

A chemical titration method described by van de Kamer, et al. in 1949 in which fecal fat is quantitatively measured by conversion of fecal lipids into fatty acids through saponification with ethanolic potassium hydroxide, release of the free fatty acids by the addition of hydrochloric acid and extraction into ether, and titration of the fatty acids against sodium hydroxide. (NCI)
A nuclear imaging test that uses radiopharmaceuticals to produce an image of the blood flow to the lungs.

An assay that is used to determine viral quantity by infecting monolayers of host cells with serially diluted virus, covering the monolayers with an immobilizing overlay after a period of incubation to restrict the spread of the virus to neighboring cells, and counting the resulting visible plaques of infected cells.
A psychometric response scale to assess subjective characteristics or symptoms, which relies upon a continuum of possible result values in between two fixed end-points.
A type of conditioned audiometry to detect sound, where a delayed visual presentation is used to support a child's reflexive orientation response to a audio signal from a single source.

A type of blood cell analysis that uses impedance, conductivity, and laser scatter to measure cell volume, cell size, chemical composition, nuclear volume, cellular granularity, nuclear structure, and cell surface characteristics.
A method for estimating body surface area of second and third degree burns, based on assigned percentages for different regions of the body.

A microscopy staining method that utilizes a modified trichrome stain to determine the presence of microspordial, sporulating species. The staining method utilizes chromotrope 2R, a red acidic dye, the counterstain fast green, and phosphotungstic acid.

A technique that assesses auditory function and/or type of hearing loss, in which a vibrating tuning fork (typically at 256Hz or 512Hz) is placed on top of the head or over the upper lip and the subject reporting whether sound is heard equally in both ears or whether the sound is louder in one ear.
A method that measures the sedimentation rate of an entity in an aqueous solution using a Westergren tube.

A method for the detection or identification of proteins or peptides that have been separated by gel electrophoresis and transferred onto nitrocellulose or other type of paper or nylon membrane. The proteins are then detected by reaction with enzymatically labeled or radiolabeled antibody probes.
A DNA sequencing technique in which all of the exons of an individual's genome are sequenced.
A DNA sequencing technique in which the entirety of the individual's genome is sequenced.
An RNA sequencing technique in which all of the RNA transcripts of an individual's genome are sequenced.

A microscopy staining method that utilizes the Romanowsky stains, eosin and methylene blue, solubilized in methanol. In this staining protocol, methanol is also utilized as a fixative agent prior to staining.

A microscopy staining method that is a combination of the Wright and Giemsa staining protocols and utilizes the Romanowsky stains, which are mixtures of eosin and thiazine dyes such as methylene blue. It produces darker blue and magenta shades than the giemsa stain alone, which may provide better contrast in microscopy.

A spectrometric method that determines the type and concentration of elements or chemicals in a sample, based upon the principle that each element emits fluorescent light of a particular wavelength when exposed to an X-ray.
A type of X-ray in which the images are not enhanced by the addition of contrast agents into the body.
A radiographic procedure using the emission of x-rays, a type of penetrating energy wave.

A microscopy acid fast staining method that utilizes Ziehl-Neelsen carbol fuchsin, acid alcohol and methylene blue, to determine the presence of acid fast microorganisms. This acid fast staining technique requires heating during the primary staining step involving the carbol fuchsin.
terms.preferredTerm: Ziehl Neelsen Acid Fast Staining Method

terms.definition: Cannot distinguish between two or more possible values in the current context. (NCI)

The growth of microorganisms may be inhibited by antimicrobials that approach usually attainable blood and tissue concentrations. The response rates may be lower than for susceptible isolates. This category also includes a buffer zone, which should prevent small, uncontrolled, technical factors from causing major discrepancies in interpretations, especially for drugs with narrow pharmacotoxicity margins.

A category used for microorganisms that have only a susceptible interpretive category, but not an intermediate or resistant interpretive category (i.e., susceptible-only interpretive category). This category may be applied to new antimicrobial agents for which no resistant microorganisms have been encountered at the time the initial interpretive criteria are determined. Microorganisms that test with an MIC above or a zone measurement below the susceptible interpretive criteria are designated as nonsusceptible. A designation of nonsusceptible does not necessarily mean that a resistance mechanism(s) exists in the microorganism.
Determination of a value is not relevant in the current context. (NCI)

The growth of the microorganism is intermediate or resistant to an antimicrobial. This category is used when describing isolates that are above the susceptible interpretive category breakpoint as defined by a standards organization, and, when the "intermediate" breakpoint and the "resistant" breakpoint are defined but not applied; or when "intermediate" and "resistant" interpretive categories are merged/combined.

The growth of microorganisms are not inhibited by the usually achievable concentrations of the antimicrobial agent with normal dosages, and/or microorganisms demonstrate MICs or zone diameters that fall in the range where specific microbial resistance mechanisms (e.g. Beta-lactamases) are likely, and clinical efficacy of the agent against the microorganism has not been reliably shown in treatment studies.
The growth of microorganisms are inhibited by the usually achievable concentrations of antimicrobial agent when the recommended dosage is used for the site of infection.
The growth of microorganisms may be inhibited when higher than normal dosages of an antimicrobial agent are used and maximal possible blood concentration of the antimicrobial agent is achieved.
Not known, not observed, not recorded, or refused. (NCI)

terms.definition: A grading system developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) and assigned based on the degree of cellular differentiation within a tumor sample.

A score developed by Allred et al. (1998) and assigned based on the percent positivity of cells for a particular analyte (Allred DC, Harvey JM, Berardo M, Clark GM. Prognostic and predictive factors in breast cancer by immunohistochemical analysis. Mod Pathol. 1998 Feb;11(2):155-68).

A score developed by Allred et al. (1998) and assigned based on the average staining intensity of cells for a particular analyte. (Allred DC, Harvey JM, Berardo M, Clark GM. Prognostic and predictive factors in breast cancer by immunohistochemical analysis. Mod Pathol. 1998 Feb;11(2):155-68)

The interpretation of the findings of the Allred Total Score, the histopathological evaluation of staining in tissue based on the Allred scoring system. Scores of 0-2 are considered negative expression and scores of 3-8 are considered positive expression. (Allred DC, Harvey JM, Berardo M, Clark GM. Prognostic and predictive factors in breast cancer by immunohistochemical analysis. Mod Pathol. 1998 Feb;11(2):155-68).

The total score within the Allred scoring system developed by Allred et al. (1998) and based on the sum of the proportion positive score and the staining intensity score. (Allred DC, Harvey JM, Berardo M, Clark GM. Prognostic and predictive factors in breast cancer by immunohistochemical analysis. Mod Pathol. 1998 Feb;11(2):155-68)
The extent of a 2-dimensional surface enclosed within a boundary. (NCI)
A measurement of the average shortest distances between the cells of interest to the boundary between the invasive margin and whole tumor region.
terms.preferredTerm: Average Shortest Distances to Invasive Margin-Whole Tumor Region Boundary Measurement
terms.submissionValue: AVERAGE SHORTEST DISTANCES TO IM-WTR BOUNDARY
synonyms: Average Shortest Distances to Invasive Margin-Whole Tumor Region Boundary

terms.definition: A score originally developed by Solez et al. (1993) and assigned based on the histologic evaluation of kidney allograft biopsies according to the Banff Working Classification of Renal Allograft Pathology.
The histopathological evaluation of the liver based on the Batts-Ludwig scoring system.

A score based on the Bauermeister scale, a 6-point grading system used to rate the extent of myelofibrosis, based on the amount of reticulin and collagen fibers present in the bone marrow. (Bauermeister DE. Quantitation of bone marrow reticulin-a normal range. Am J Clin Pathol. 1971 Jul;56(1):24-31.)

The measurement in millimeters of the vertical thickness of primary cutaneous melanoma. Breslow thickness is measured from the granular layer of the epidermis, or the ulcer base (if ulcerated), to the deepest tumor cells.
A grading system developed by the College of American Pathology to assess a decrease in tumor size or extent in the body. (College of American Pathology)
terms.preferredTerm: College of American Pathology Tumor Regression Grade
synonyms: College of American Pathology Tumor Regression Grade

terms.definition: A measurement of the total nucleated cells in a biological specimen.

A microscopic measurement of the volumetric or area ratios of components (e.g. blood vessel-, macrophage-, or lymphatic vessel density) of tissues or organs. (Chalkley HW. Method for the quantitative morphological analysis of tissues. J Natl Cancer Inst; 4: 47-52)
A relative measurement (percentage) of the number of positive staining cells to the total number of viable tumor cells.
The histopathological evaluation of the liver based on the enhanced liver fibrosis scoring system.

A morphologic classification system for prostate carcinoma with neuroendocrine differentiation by Epstein et al (2014). (Epstein JI, Amin MB, Beltran H, Lotan TL, Mosquera JM, Reuter VE, Robinson BD, Troncoso P, Rubin MA. Proposed morphologic classification of prostate cancer with neuroendocrine differentiation. Am J Surg Pathol. 2014 Jun;38(6):756-67.)

A score based on the European Consensus scale, a 4-point grading system for the qualitative and quantitative evaluation of bone marrow fibrosis. (Thiele J, Kvasnicka HM, Facchetti F, Franco V, van der Walt J, Orazi A. European consensus on grading bone marrow fibrosis and assessment of cellularity. Haematologica. 2005 Aug;90(8):1128-32.)
terms.preferredTerm: European Consensus Score For Bone Marrow Fibrosis

terms.definition: A grading system developed by Evans et al (1992) to assess a decrease in tumor size or extent in the body. (Evans DB, Rich TA, Byrd DR, Cleary KR, Connelly JH, Levin B, et al. Preoperative chemoradiation and pancreaticoduodenectomy for adenocarcinoma of the pancreas. Arch Surg. (1992) 127:1335-9.)
terms.preferredTerm: Evans et al Tumor Regression Grade (1992)

terms.definition: A classification for grading and staging of acute leukemias published by the French-American-British (FAB) co-operative group in 1985. (Bennett JM, Catovsky D, Daniel MT, et al. Proposed revised criteria for the classification of acute myeloid leukemia. A report of the French-American-British Cooperative Group. Ann Intern Med. 1985;103(4):620-625.)

A tumor histopathologic grading system developed by Bhatla et al (2018) for uterine and cervical cancers. (Bhatla N, Aoki D, Sharma DN, Sankaranarayanan R. Cancer of the cervix uteri. Int J Gynaecol Obstet 2018;143(Suppl 2):22-36.)

A tumor grading system developed by Fuhrman et al (1982) that evaluates nuclear grade, based on nuclear size, irregularity and nucleolar prominence, in renal cell carcinomas. (Fuhrman SA, Lasky SA, Limas C. Prognostic significance of morphologic parameters in renal cell carcinoma. Am J Surg Pathol. 1982 Oct;6(7):655-63.)

A score originally developed by D'Haens et al. (1998) and assigned based on the histologic evaluation of acute and chronic inflammatory changes, epithelial damage, and the extent of inflammation in Crohn's disease mucosal biopsy specimens, according to the Global Histologic Disease Activity Score. (G R D'Haens, K Geboes, M Peeters, F Baert, F Penninckx, P Rutgeerts. Early lesions of recurrent Crohn's disease caused by infusion of intestinal contents in excluded ileum. Gastroenterology. 1998 Feb;114(2):262-7).

Philadelphia: Lea and Febiger. pp. 171-198.)

The Veteran's Administration Cooperative Urologic Research Group: histologic grading and clinical staging of prostatic carcinoma. In Tannenbaum, M. Urologic Pathology: The Prostate. Philadelphia: Lea and Febiger. pp. 171-198.)

The sum of the primary and secondary Gleason scores. If three patterns are identified, it is the sum of the primary pattern score and the score of the least well-differentiated pattern. (Gleason, D. F. (1977). The Veteran's Administration Cooperative Urologic Research Group: histologic grading and clinical staging of prostatic carcinoma. In Tannenbaum, M. Urologic Pathology: The Prostate. Philadelphia: Lea and Febiger. pp. 171-198.)

The Two Histological Main Types Of Gastric Carcinoma: Diffuse And So-Called Intestinal-Type Carcinoma. An Attempt At A Histo-Clinical Classification. (LAUREN P. terms.preferredTerm: C4 Enriched Glutamine to Total Glutamine Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: A measurement of the glutamine in a biological specimen.
A relative measurement (ratio or percentage) of the glutamine to creatine in a biological specimen.
A measurement of the glycerophosphorylcholine (GPC) plus phosphorylcholine (PC) in a biological specimen.
An evaluation of graphesthesia (the ability to recognize symbols when they're traced on the skin).
A relative measurement (ratio or percentage) of the lactate to creatine in a biological specimen.

An involuntary, primal response in the neonate to loud noise or the feeling of falling. The response is characterized by the infant's arms symmetrically spreading out to the side and then back to the midline, and involuntarily flexing the fingers and toes.
An evaluation of muscular rigidity (an involuntary, persistent state of firm, tense muscles with marked resistance to passive movement).
A measurement of the myo-inositol in a biological specimen.
A relative measurement (ratio or percentage) of the myo-inositol to creatine in a biological specimen.
A measurement of the N-acetyl aspartate in a biological specimen.
A relative measurement (ratio) of the N-acetyl aspartate to the choline in a biological specimen.
terms.preferredTerm: N-Acetyl Aspartate to Choline Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: A relative measurement (ratio) of the N-acetyl aspartate to the creatine in a biological specimen.
terms.preferredTerm: N-Acetyl Aspartate to Creatine Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: A relative measurement (ratio) of the N-acetyl aspartate to the creatinine plus choline to the creatine in a biological specimen.
terms.preferredTerm: N-Acetyl Aspartate to Creatine and Choline Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: The length of time of N1 sleep.
A relative measurement (percentage) of the N1 sleep time to total sleep time.
terms.preferredTerm: N1 Sleep to Total Sleep Time Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: An assessment of the latency of the N145 or N2 wave of the visual evoked potential assessment waveform.
The length of time of N2 sleep.
A relative measurement (percentage) of the N2 sleep time to total sleep time.
terms.preferredTerm: N2 Sleep to Total Sleep Time Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: The length of time of N3 sleep.
A relative measurement (percentage) of the N3 sleep time to total sleep time.
terms.preferredTerm: N3 Sleep to Total Sleep Time Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: An assessment of the latency of the N75 or N1 wave of the visual evoked potential assessment waveform.
A measurement of the N-acetylaspartate plus N-acetyl-aspartylglutamate in a biological specimen.
An observation, assessment or examination of the nervous system.
The magnitude, or height, of the P100 wave of the visual evoked potential assessment waveform. This assessment calculates the height from the N75 negative peak to the P100 positive peak.
terms.preferredTerm: N75 to P100 Peak to Peak Amplitude

terms.definition: An assessment of the latency of the P100 or P1 wave of the visual evoked potential assessment waveform.
An involuntary, primal response in the neonate to grasp the fingers when their palm is touched. This reflex is present until six months of age.
A measurement of the time interval between a stimulus and the maximal response.
The maximum height change between the wave and the equilibrium point of a stimulus-response waveform.
An involuntary, primal response in the neonate that is characterized by flexion of the toes when the sole of the foot is stroked.
An evaluation of postural tremor (involuntary and rhythmic shaking of a body part that is held against gravity).
The total amount of time an individual spends in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.
terms.preferredTerm: Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Phase Duration

terms.definition: The time between the onset of sleep and the onset of the first rapid eye movement (REM) cycle.
terms.preferredTerm: Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Phase Latency

terms.definition: A relative measurement (percentage) of the rapid eye movement (REM) sleep time to total sleep time.
terms.preferredTerm: REM to Total Sleep Time Ratio Measurement

terms.definition: An evaluation of resting tremor (involuntary and rhythmic shaking of a body part that is relaxed and not held against gravity, and where the tremor amplitude decreases with voluntary movements).
An involuntary, primal response in the neonate to search for the nipple when the cheek is touched.
The degree to which the skin can conduct electricity.
A relative measurement (percentage) of the total sleep time (N1 sleep + N2 sleep + N3 sleep + REM sleep) to the total time spent in bed.
The duration of time between when the lights are turned off and when the individual falls asleep.
The ratio between the uptake or binding of a radiopharmaceutical agent in an anatomical region of interest and a context-defined reference anatomical region.
The ratio between the tissue radioactivity concentration at a point in time C(T) and the injected dose of radioactivity per kilogram of the patient's body weight.
An involuntary, primal response in the neonate to take brisk steps when the feet are placed on a surface whilst in a supported standing position.
An involuntary, primal response in the neonate when a nipple is placed on an infant's lips.
The dimension between two surfaces of an object, usually the smallest dimension as opposed to the width or the length.
The total amount of sleep time from sleep onset to sleep offset, determined by summing the N1 sleep, N2 sleep, N3 sleep, and REM sleep durations.
An evaluation of tremor (the shaking movement of the whole body or just a certain part of it, often caused by problems of the neurons responsible for muscle action).
A measurement of the metabolic rate of the tricarboxylic acid cycle in a biological specimen.
A measurement of the amount of three dimensional space occupied by an object or the capacity of a space or container.
A measurement of the sum of durations of wakefulness episodes throughout the night, not including the wakefulness before sleep onset.

terms.definition: Neuropathic Pain Scale - Please use the scale below to tell us how cold your pain feels. Words used to describe very cold pain included 'like ice' and 'freezing.'

terms.definition: Neuropathic Pain Scale - Please use the scale below to tell us how itchy your pain feels. Words used to describe itchy pain include 'like poison oak' and 'like a mosquito bite.'

terms.definition: Neuropathic Pain Scale - Which of the following best describes the time quality of your pain? Please check only one answer.

synonyms: NPS01-Describe Time Quality Of Your Pain

terms.definition: Neuropathic Pain Scale - I feel a background pain all of the time and occasional flare-ups (break-through pain) some of the time. Describe the background pain.
Neuropathic Pain Scale - I feel a background pain all of the time and occasional flare-ups (break-through pain) some of the time. Describe the flare-up (break-through) pain.
Neuropathic Pain Scale - I feel a single type of pain all the time. Describe this pain.
terms.preferredTerm: NPS - Describe the Single Type of Pain All Time
synonyms: NPS01-Describe Single Type Pain All Time

terms.definition: Neuropathic Pain Scale - I fee a single type of pain only sometimes. Other times, I am pain free. Describe the occasional pain.

Neuropathic Pain Scale - Now that you have told us the different physical aspects of your pain, the different types of sensations, we want you to tell us overall how unpleasant your pain is to you. Words used to describe very unpleasant pain include 'miserable' and intolerable.' Remember, pain can have a low intensity, buy still feel extremely unpleasant, and some kinds of pain can have a high intensity but be very tolerable. With this scale, please tell us how unpleasant your pain feels.
terms.preferredTerm: NPS - Tell Us Overall How Unpleasant Your Pain is to You
synonyms: NPS01-Tell How Unpleasant Your Pain Feel

terms.definition: Neuropathic Pain Scale - Lastly, we want you to give us an estimate of the severity of your deep versus surface pain. We want your to rate each location of pain separately. terms.preferredTerm: NPS - How Intense is Your Deep Pain

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have beliefs that you know are not true? (for example, insisting that people are trying to harm him/her or steal from him/her)? Has he/she said that family members are not who they say they are or that the house is not their home? I'm not asking about mere suspiciousness; I am interested if the patient is convinced that these things are happening to him/her.
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Have Beliefs That You Know are Not True

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that he/she is in danger - that others are planning to hurt him/her?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that others are stealing from him/her?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Others are Stealing From Him/Her

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that his/her spouse is having an affair?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - His/Her Spouse is Having an Affair

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that unwelcome guests are living in his/her house?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Unwelcome Guests are Living in His/Her House

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that his/her spouse or others are not who they claim to be?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - His/Her Spouse or Others Are Not Who They Claim To Be

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that his/her house is not his/her home?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - His/Her House Is Not His/Her Home

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that family members plan to abandon him/her?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Family Members Plan to Abandon Him/Her

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe that television or magazine figures are actually present in the home? (Does he/she try to talk or interact with them?)
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Television or Magazine Figures Are Actually Present In the Home

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient believe any other unusual things that I haven't asked about?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Any Other Unusual Things That I Haven't Asked About

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Frequency of the delusions.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Severity of the delusions.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - How emotionally distressing do you find this behavior?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Delusions: (frequency score x severity score).

Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have hallucinations such as seeing false visions or hearing false voices? Does he/she seem to see, hear or experience things that are not present? By this question we do not mean just mistaken beliefs such as stating that someone who has died is still alive; rather we are asking if the patient actually has abnormal experiences of sounds or visions.
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Hallucinations Such as Seeing False Visions or Hearing False Voices

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient describe hearing voices or act as if he/she hears voices?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Describe Hearing Voices or Act as if He/She Hears Voices

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient talk to people who are not there?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Talk to People Who Are Not There

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient describe seeing things not seen by others or behave as if he/she is seeing things not seen by others (people, animals, lights, etc.)?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Describe Seeing Things Not Seen by Others
synonyms: NPI1-See Things Not Seen by Others

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient report smelling odors not smelled by others?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Report Smelling Odors Not Smelled by Others
synonyms: NPI1-Smell Odors Others Do Not Smell

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient describe feeling things on his/her skin or otherwise appear to be feeling things crawling or touching him/her?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Describe Feeling Things on His/Her Skin

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient describe tastes that are without any known cause?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Describe Tastes That Are Without Any Known Cause

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient describe any other unusual sensory experiences?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Describe Any Other Unusual Sensory Experiences

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Frequency of the hallucinations.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Severity of the hallucinations.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - How emotionally distressing do you find this behavior?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Hallucinations: (frequency score x severity score).
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have periods when he/she refuses to cooperate or won't let people help him/her? Is he/she hard to handle?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Periods When He/She Refuses to Cooperate

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient get upset with those trying to care for him/her or resist activities such as bathing or changing clothes?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Get Upset with Those Trying to Care for Him/Her

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Is the patient stubborn, having to have things his/her way?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Is the patient uncooperative, resistive to help from others?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have any other behaviors that make him/her hard to handle?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Any Other Behaviors That Make Him/Her Hard to Handle

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient shout or curse angrily?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient slam doors, kick furniture, throw things?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Slam doors, Kick Furniture, Throw Things

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient attempt to hurt or hit others?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Attempt to Hurt or Hit Others

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have any other aggressive or agitated behaviors?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Any Other Aggressive or Agitated Behaviors

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Frequency of the agitation/aggression.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Severity of the agitation/aggression.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - How emotionally distressing do you find this behavior?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Agitation/Aggression: (frequency score x severity score).
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient seem sad or depressed? Does he/she say that he/she feels sad or depressed?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have periods of tearfulness or sobbing that seem to indicate sadness?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Periods of Tearfulness or Sobbing

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient say, or act as if he/she is sad or in low spirits?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Say, or Act as if He/She is Sad or in Low Spirits
synonyms: NPI1-Say or Act in Low Spirits

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient put him/herself down or say that he/she feels like a failure?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Put Him/Herself Down or Say That He/She Feels Like a Failure

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient say that he/she is a bad person or deserves to be punished?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Say That He/She is a Bad Person

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient seem very discouraged or say that he/she has no future?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient say he/she is a burden to the family or that the family would be better off without him/her?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Say He/She is a Burden to the Family

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient express a wish for death or talk about killing himself/herself?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Express a Wish for Death

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient show any other signs of depression or sadness?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Show Any Other Signs of Depression or Sadness

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Frequency of the depression/dysphoria.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Severity of the depression/dysphoria.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - How emotionally distressing do you find this behavior?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Depression/Dysphoria: (frequency score x severity score).
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Sub-total of distress score.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Is the patient very nervous, worried, or frightened for no apparent reason? Does he/she seem very tense or fidgety? Is the patient afraid to be apart from you?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Very Nervous, Worried, or Frightened for No Apparent Reason

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient say that he/she is worried about planned events?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Say That He/She is Worried About Planned Events

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have periods of feeling shaky, unable to relax, or feeling excessively tense?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Periods of Feeling Shaky, Unable to Relax, or Feeling Excessively Tense

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient have periods of (or complain of) shortness of breath, gasping, or sighing for no apparent reason other than nervousness?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Periods of Shortness of Breath, Gasping, or Sighing for No Apparent Reason

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient complain of butterflies in his/her stomach, or of racing or pounding of the heart in association with nervousness? (Symptoms not explained by ill health).
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Complain of Butterflies, Racing or Pounding Heart

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient avoid certain places or situations that make him/her more nervous such as riding in the car, meeting with friends, or being in crowds?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Avoid Certain Places or Situations That Make Him/Her More Nervous

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient become nervous and upset when separated from you (or his/her caregiver)? (Does he/she cling to you to keep from being separated?).
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Become Nervous and Upset When Separated From You

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient show any other signs of anxiety?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Show Any Other Signs of Anxiety

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Frequency of the anxiety.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Severity of the anxiety.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - How emotionally distressing do you find this behavior?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Anxiety: (frequency score x severity score).

Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient seem too cheerful or too happy for no reason? I don't mean the normal happiness that comes from seeing friends, receiving presents, or spending time with family members. I am asking if the patient has a persistent and abnormally good mood or finds humor where others do not.
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Seem Too Cheerful or Too Happy for No Reason

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient appear to feel good or to be too happy, different from his/her usual self?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Appear to Feel Good or to Be Too Happy

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient find humor and laugh at things that others do not find funny?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Fine Humor and Laugh at Things That Others Do Not Find Funny
synonyms: NPI1-Humor Others Do Not Find Funny

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient seem to have a childish sense of humor with a tendency to giggle or laugh inappropriately (such as when something unfortunate happens to others)?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Seem to Have a Childish Sense of Humor

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient tell jokes or make remarks that are not funny to others but seem funny to him/her?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Tell Jokes or Make Remarks That are Not Funny to Others
synonyms: NPI1-Jokes Others Do Not Find Funny

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does he/she play childish pranks such as pinching or playing "keep away" for the fun of it?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient "talk big" or claim to have more abilities or wealth than is true?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Talk Big or Claim to Have More Abilities or Wealth Than is True

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient show any other signs of feeling too good or being too happy?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Show Any Other Signs of Feeling Too Good or Being Too Happy
synonyms: NPI1-Other Signs of Feeling Too Happy

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Frequency of the elation/euphoria.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Severity of the elation/euphoria.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - How emotionally distressing do you find this behavior?
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Elation/Euphoria: (frequency score x severity score).

Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Has the patient lost interest in the world around him/her? Has he/she lost interest in doing things or does he/she lack motivation for starting new activities? Is he/she more difficult to engage in conversation or in doing chores? Is the patient apathetic or indifferent?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Lost Interest in the World Around Him/Her

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient seem less spontaneous and less active than usual?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Seem Less Spontaneous and Less Active Than Usual

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Is the patient less likely to initiate a conversation?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Less Likely Initiate to Initiate a Conversation

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Is the patient less affectionate or lacking in emotions when compared to his/her usual self?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Less Affectionate or Lacking in Emotions

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient contribute less to household chores?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Contribute Less to Household Chores

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient seem less interested in the activities and plans of others?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Less Interested in the Activities and Plans of Others

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Has the patient lost interest in friends and family members?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Lost Interest in Friends and Family Members

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Is the patient less enthusiastic about his/her usual interests?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Less Enthusiastic About His/Her Usual Interests

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Does the patient show any other signs that he/she doesn't care about doing new things?
terms.preferredTerm: NPI - Show Any Other Signs That He/She Doesn't Care About Doing New Things

terms.definition: Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Frequency of the apathy/indifference.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory - Severity of the apathy/indifference.

terms.definition: An AUC calculation method that utilizes the linear trapezoidal interpolation rule up to the maximum concentration (Cmax) and Logarithmic trapezoidal interpolation for the remainder of the concentration curve.

An AUC calculation method that utilizes the linear trapezoidal interpolation rule for the entire concentration curve, except when partial areas are selected with no measured endpoint, then logarithmic interpolation is used to calculate the missing data.
An AUC calculation method that utilizes the linear trapezoidal interpolation rule for the entire concentration curve.

An AUC calculation method that utilizes linear trapezoidal interpolation between two points any time the measured concentration increases and logarithmic trapezoidal interpolation between two points any time the concentration decreases over the entire concentration curve.

terms.definition: The fraction of the treatment dose that reaches the systemic circulation; this is the ratio of the amount of drug in the system (area under the curve) after extravascular administration of a test formulation divided by the drug in the system (area under the curve) after IV administration.

The area under the curve (AUC) extrapolated to infinity, calculated using the observed value of the last non-zero concentration divided by the area under the curve (AUC) extrapolated to infinity, calculated using the observed value of the last non-zero concentration during the initial dosing interval.

The area under the curve (AUC) extrapolated to infinity, calculated using the predicted value of the last non-zero concentration divided by the area under the curve (AUC) extrapolated to infinity, calculated using the predicted value of the last non-zero concentration during the initial dosing interval.
The area under the curve from T1 to T2 at steady state divided by the area under the curve from T1 to T2 during the initial dosing interval, each divided by the associated dose.

The ability to move body parts and limbs without physical restriction. (NCI)

codelists.definition: A terminology codelist to describe any activity considered to be a therapeutic or diagnostic procedure.
codelists.name: Procedure
codelists.preferredTerm: CDISC SDTM Procedure Terminology

terms.definition: A process by which a dose of radiation is automatically shaped to closely conform to the entire volume of the tumor, so that surrounding normal tissue is spared and treatment toxicity is decreased. (NCI)
Removal, separation, detachment, extirpation or eradication of a body part, pathway or function by surgery, chemical destruction, morbid process, or noxious substance. (NCI)
An invasive therapeutic procedure to destroy tissue in an accessory pathways in the atrioventricular conduction system that contributes to arrhythmia.
An invasive therapeutic procedure to destroy tissue in the cardiac atria that is the source of an arrhythmia.
An invasive therapeutic procedure to destroy tissue in the AV-node that contributes to arrhythmia.
An invasive therapeutic procedure to destroy tissue in the heart used to correct heart arrhythmias.
Removal, separation, detachment, extirpation or eradication of a body part, pathway or function by chemical means. (NCI)
Removal, separation, detachment, extirpation or eradication of a body part, pathway or function by light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. (NCI)
An invasive therapeutic procedure to destroy tissue in the cardiac ventricles that is the source of an arrhythmia.
Stem cell transfer or transplantation from a donor other than one's self.
Dilation of the valve between the left ventricle of the heart and the aorta by inflating a balloon.
Surgery performed with the purpose of replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, dysfunctional, etc. aortic valve with a bioprosthetic, homograft, or autograft valve.
Implantation of a prosthetic device into the body to replace the function of both cardiac ventricles and all four cardiac valves, typically as a bridge to transplantation.
Repair of atrial septum.
Stem cell transfer or transplantation in which the patient is their own donor.
A type of non-invasive mechanical ventilation procedure that that uses bilevel positive airway pressure to support spontaneous breathing activity.
Surgical removal of two lobes of the right lung.
The removal of tissue specimens or fluid from the living body for microscopic examination, performed to establish a diagnosis.
A type of biopsy in which a tissue sample is removed using a needle with a relatively large diameter.
A type of biopsy in which an entire lesion is removed for microscopic examination.
A type of biopsy in which part of a lesion is removed for microscopic examination.
A type of biopsy in which a disk of tissue is removed using a punch device.
A surgical procedure in which a cardiac pacing device with a built-in cardioverter defibrillator is placed under the skin, with leads positioned in the right atrium and both ventricles.
A mechanical fluid removal technique that involves the pressure-driven movement of plasma water and solutes from whole blood across a semipermeable membrane.
A therapeutic procedure to replace diseased or pathologic bone marrow with transplanted, healthy bone marrow cells.
A type of radiation therapy in which radioactive material is placed inside the body, into a tumor or body cavity.
A type of brachytherapy in which radioactive material sealed in needles, seeds, wires, or catheters is placed directly into a tumor or body tissue.
A type of brachytherapy in which radioactive material sealed in needles, seeds, wires, or catheters is placed directly into a body cavity such as the chest cavity or the vagina.
Any of a number of implantable cardiac devices meant to aid the heart in carrying out its functions.
A procedure in which a thin plastic tube (catheter) is inserted into an artery or vein in the arm or leg and then advanced into the chambers of the heart or into the coronary arteries.
An invasive procedure that includes an electronic device that stimulates both right and left cardiac ventricles to improve coordination of ventricular contraction.

A procedure performed during a percutaneous coronary intervention in which a device is deployed into the lumen of a coronary artery to expand and support the vessel wall such that the vessel remains patent and blood flow is uninhibited.
A surgical procedure in which a damaged heart is removed and replaced by another heart from a suitable donor.
The administration of pharmacologic agents to correct abnormal heart rhythm.
The administration of electric current to correct abnormal heart rhythm.
A surgical procedure to remove the clouded lens from the eye, and oftentimes replace it with an artificial lens.
The use of synthetic or naturally-occurring chemicals for the treatment of diseases.
Surgical removal of the gallbladder.
Endoscopic examination of the luminal surface of the colon.
A type of non-invasive mechanical ventilation procedure that uses continuous positive airway pressure to support spontaneous breathing activity.
A type of ECG gated MRI in which the images are enhanced by the addition of contrast agents into the body.

A procedure performed to bypass partially or completely occluded coronary arteries with veins and/or arteries harvested from elsewhere in the body, thereby improving the blood supply to the coronary circulation supplying the myocardium (heart muscle).
Removal, separation, detachment, extirpation or eradication of a body part, pathway or function by freezing. (NCI)
The therapeutic use of cold or refrigeration.
An imaging technique for examining structures within the body by scanning them with X rays and using a computer to construct a series of cross-sectional scans along a single axis.
The removal of tissue with a curette (a spoon-shaped instrument with a sharp edge).
A type of digital fundus photography that makes use of a significantly wider viewing angle than traditional fundus photography.
A type of ECG gated MRI in which the images are not enhanced by the addition of contrast agents into the body.
A type of magnetic resonance imaging in which data is acquired during a specified portion of the cardiac cycle, allowing for the collection of stop motion imaging of the heart.
A procedure for destroying tissue using an electrical current.
Excision of an atheromatous plaque. (NCI)
An endoscopic procedure that visualizes the upper part of the gastrointestinal tract up to and including the duodenum.
The act of cutting out; the surgical removal of part or all of a structure or organ. (NCI)
Creation of a surgical opening into the abdominal cavity for examination of the contents of the abdominal cavity as a means of diagnosis.
A type of radiation therapy in which high-energy beams are delivered to the tumor from outside of the body.
The use of an adsorbing hemofilter in an external blood purification device to reduce cytokine levels in the blood.
A technique that utilizes a device to pump a patient's blood outside of the body, oxygenate it, and return it to the body.
Any surgical procedure performed for the purpose of repairing or replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, or dysfunctional heart valve.
A therapeutic procedure that involves the transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells, either with the patient as their own donor or from a donor to a patient.
A therapeutic procedure involving the extracorporeal removal of harmful waste and fluids from the blood using a dialysis machine. Following dialysis, the blood is returned to the body.

A mechanical fluid removal technique that involves the pressure-driven movement of plasma water and solutes from whole blood through a system of extracorporeal filters, with simultaneous reinfusion of replacement fluid into the body to keep volume homeostasis.
A type of brachytherapy that targets a cancerous tissue with high doses of radiation through the use of inserted temporary implants.
The delivery of heated, humidified, oxygen-enriched gas via nasal cannula at flow rates greater than those typically delivered by standard-flow oxygen devices.

An electrocardiographic method for collecting continuous ECG waveforms with a variable number of discrete leads with duration longer than the standard 10 second ECG. Holter recording may be performed in patients who are ambulatory, and may collect data for 24 hours or longer.
A therapy designed to induce changes in a patient's immune status.
A procedure involving an electronic device implanted in the body that delivers electrical stimulation to the heart to treat tachycardia. It may also have the capability to treat bradycardia.
The use of an intense beam of light, such as a laser, to seal off blood vessels or destroy tissue. (NCI)

An advanced form of 3-Dimensional Conformal Radiation Therapy (3D CRT) that involves the use of varying intensities of small radiation beams to produce dosage distributions that are more precise than those possible with 3D CRT. (NCI)

A type of mechanical circulatory support procedure in which a balloon catheter inserted into the proximal descending aorta is inflated immediately after aortic valve closure in diastole and deflated just before aortic valve opening in systole, with the augmentation of coronary blood flow during diastole increasing coronary blood flow and systemic perfusion.
A type of mechanical ventilation procedure that uses an invasive means, such as an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy tube, to deliver oxygenated air into the lungs.
A procedure involving one or more wires used for pacemaker or implantable defibrillator devices.
The therapeutic blockage of the muscular pouch in the left atrium.
terms.preferredTerm: Intentional Left Cardiac Atrial Appendage Occlusion Procedure

terms.definition: Surgical removal of the left portion of the colon.
A procedure involving the implantation of a mechanical cardiac pump which receives blood from the left ventricle and delivers it to the aorta. (NCI)
An examination and assessment of the inability of the left ventricle to effectively pump blood to the body.
terms.preferredTerm: Left Cardiac Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction Evaluation

terms.definition: Surgical removal of a lobe of an organ.
Any immunotherapy that targets, or is restricted to, a specific anatomical location.
Resection of the rectum through an incision in the lower abdomen.
A type of brachytherapy that targets a cancerous tissue with low doses of radiation through the use of inserted temporary or permanent implants.
Surgical removal of a discrete mass.
Surgical removal of the lymph node(s).

A procedure that mechanically assists or replaces spontaneous breathing in patients by use of a powered device that forces oxygenated air into or out of the lungs through positive and/or negative pressure.
Surgical removal of metastases.
Any therapeutic procedure in which microwave irradiation is used for the purpose of heating and destroying targeted tissue.
Dilation of the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle of the heart by inflating a balloon.
Dilation of the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle of the heart by use of a surgeon's finger or rigid instrument.
Surgery performed for the purpose of reducing regurgitation of the mitral valve.
Surgery performed with the purpose of replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, dysfunctional, etc. mitral valve with bioprosthetic, homograft or autograft valve.
Surgical removal of one or both breasts, including the areola, nipple, and the majority of the axillary lymph nodes, but sparing the pectoralis major muscle.

A dermatologic procedure used to treat certain forms of skin cancer in which tissue is removed and immediately tested via frozen section; tissue continues to be removed until clear margins are achieved.

Imaging that uses radiofrequency waves and a strong magnetic field rather than x-rays to provide amazingly clear and detailed pictures of internal organs and tissues. The technique is valuable for the diagnosis of many pathologic conditions, including cancer, heart and vascular disease, stroke, and joint and musculoskeletal disorders.
A multi-gated acquisition (MUGA) scan and a form of radionuclide imaging that provides a comprehensive look at blood flow and the function of the lower chambers of the heart ventricles.
An operative procedure that does not involve the heart or the blood vessels.
A type of mechanical ventilation procedure that uses a non-invasive means, such as a face mask or nasal mask, to deliver oxygenated air into the lungs.
A procedure involving an electronic device that delivers electrical stimulation to the heart to treat bradycardia.
Placement of a stent within the pancreas.
Surgical removal of the head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine (duodenum), the gallbladder and the bile duct. (Mayo Clinic)

A biospecimen collection and staining procedure in which secretions and superficial cells of the cervix are collected and stained with the Papanicolaou stain followed by microscopic examination to identify the presence of abnormal cells.
Surgical removal of part of the pancreas.

A percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the placement of an angioplasty guide wire, balloon, or other device (e.g. stent, atherectomy, brachytherapy, or thrombectomy catheter) into a native coronary artery or coronary artery bypass graft for the purpose of mechanical coronary revascularization. Examples of things not considered to be PCI procedures include intravascular ultrasound, measurements of coronary flow reserve, or measurements of fractional flow reserve.
Invasive procedure through a puncture in the skin, performed for the purpose of reducing regurgitation of the mitral valve.

A minimally invasive procedure in which a catheter is inserted into the femoral artery or vein in order to temporarily connect a mechanical circulatory support device that is worn outside the body to the circulatory system.
Removal or resection of the pericardium.
A procedure in which an opening is made in the pericardium.
The aspiration of excess fluid between the pericardium and the heart.
A therapeutic procedure that involves the transplantation of stem cells harvested from the circulating blood of a patient or donor.

A peripheral vascular intervention is a catheter-based or open surgical procedure designed to improve arterial or venous blood flow or otherwise modify or revise vascular conduits. In general, the intention to perform percutaneous vascular intervention is denoted by the insertion of a guide wire into an artery or vein. For the sake of simplicity, this definition applies to the extracranial carotid artery and other non-cardiac arteries and veins, while it excludes the lymphatics and intracranial vessels.
The collection of blood from a vein, most commonly via needle venipuncture.
Use of light and photosensitizing agents to treat cancer and other conditions.
The process by which an image is acquired by recording light emissions.
The treatment of a disorder by exposure to light, including ultraviolet and infrared radiation. (Bartleby.com)
A systemic evaluation of the body and its functions using visual inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation.
The surgical removal of all or part of the pleura. (NCI)
A therapeutic surgical procedure in which the pleural space is surgically eliminated by the adherence of the visceral and parietal pleurae. (NCI)
Surgical removal of a polypoid lesion from the mucosal surface.
Any type of non-invasive mechanical ventilation procedure that uses positive airway pressure to support spontaneous breathing activity.
Surgery performed with the purpose of replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, dysfunctional, etc. pulmonary valve with bioprosthetic, homograft or autograft valve.
Dilation of the valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery of the heart by inflating a balloon.
Surgical removal of one or both breasts, including the areola, nipple, axillary lymph nodes, and pectoral muscles.
Use of targeted or whole body radiation to treat a disease.
Surgical removal of a structure or organ, which was not completely removed in an earlier attempt.
Surgical restoration of form and/or function of a body part.
Any of the procedures used to supplement or substitute for the blood-filtering function of the kidneys.
Surgical removal of the right portion of the colon.
A procedure involving the implantation of a mechanical pump which receives blood from the right ventricle and delivers it to the pulmonary artery.
Surgical removal of a segment of an organ or partial resection of a gland.
Surgical removal and examination of the lymph node which is first in receiving the lymphatic drainage of a specified anatomic location.

A cardiac catheterization procedure to relieve symptoms in patients with severe obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A catheter is used to inject alcohol into a septal artery supplying the heart muscle responsible for the obstruction, destroying the muscle tissue and relieving the obstruction.
Surgical removal of thin slices of tissue from a structure or organ, done with a razor blade or scalpel.
Surgical removal of the sigmoid colon.
A dual-modality imaging technique that merges data from single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and computed tomography (CT) to provide structural and functional information.
terms.preferredTerm: Single Photon Tomography and Computed Tomography Scan

terms.definition: The creation of an artificially induced skin blister by the application of mechanical pressure to an area of skin, causing in vivo separation of the epidermis and dermis.
A cardiac procedure intended to inhibit atrial fibrillation, in which a series of incisions are made in the atria to block abnormal electrical circuits that contribute to atrial fibrillation.
The removal of excess fluid via needle puncture from the thoracic cavity.
A minimally invasive surgical procedure in which video-assisted thoracoscopy is used to remove of a wedge-shaped portion of tissue from a lung lobe.
terms.preferredTerm: Thorascopic Wedge Resection of the Lung

terms.definition: Surgical removal of the entire colon.
Surgical removal of the entire pancreas.
Creation of a surgical opening into the trachea.
Use of a thin tube to deliver an artificial valve apparatus between the left ventricle of the heart and the aorta.
An interventional radiologic procedure in which a shunt is placed in the liver to establish communication between the portal vein and hepatic vein for the treatment of portal hypertension.
A non-invasive cardiac ultrasound performed by placing the transducer on the chest.
A surgical procedure in which a resectoscope is passed through the urethra into the bladder to diagnose and remove all or part of a bladder tumor.
Surgical removal of the transverse colon.
Surgery performed for the purpose of reducing regurgitation of the cardiac valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.
Surgery performed with the purpose of replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, dysfunctional, etc. tricuspid valve with bioprosthetic, homograft or autograft valve.
A therapeutic procedure that involves the transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells collected from the umbilical cord or placenta.
Cardiac surgical procedure performed for the removal of an aneurysm from the ventricular wall.
Repair of ventricular septum.
A radiographic procedure using the emission of x-rays, a type of penetrating energy wave.

codelists.definition: A terminology codelist that describes the degree of urgency for a procedure.
codelists.name: Procedure Urgency Status
codelists.preferredTerm: CDISC SDTM Procedure Urgency Status Terminology

terms.definition: Elective procedures can be deferred without increased risk of compromised outcome. Patient's clinical condition is currently stable and has been stable in the days/weeks prior. The clinical situation does not demand that the procedure take place at a specified time.

Emergency procedures must be performed as soon as possible because of substantial concerns that delay could lead to death. Clinical situation demands that procedure should be performed immediately or in next available room, even if it means another case must be rescheduled.

Performing a salvage procedure is the last resort. The clinical situation involves either ongoing life support measures, life support measures for more than 60 seconds during the prior 10 minutes, or unanticipated institution of extracorporeal circulatory support.

Deferring an urgent procedure increases risk of adverse outcome or clinical deterioration. Clinical situation warrants performing urgent procedures during the current episode of care to avoid compromising patient safety.
